questions.text: How should MEP scope affect classification under this local-source article?

options.text: It automatically makes the project Group 5
It may be relevant only if it supports a source-based complexity and group-description rationale

questions.rationale: The source supports complexity and constraints, not an automatic MEP escalation rule.
questions.explanation: Describes Group 1–2 simple systems (basic forced-air ventilation and standard distribution), not the specialized systems required for Group 5 monumental facilities. Describes moderate residential or commercial systems, which are less complex than the specialized MEP scope appropriate for Group 5 civic and monumental structures. Contradicts the classification entirely; all monumental buildings require sophisticated mechanical and electrical systems. Group 5 (Monumental Buildings and Facilities — government buildings, convention centers, public facilities) requires sophisticated MEP systems including chilled water plants, variable frequency drives, and building automation systems appropriate to their scale and importance as landmark structures. Group 5 monumental buildings demand specialized MEP systems (chilled water, VFDs, building automation) commensurate with their civic significance and complexity.

questions.text: How should specialized consultants influence classification?

options.text: Consultant count alone decides the group
Consultants may evidence complexity, but the final group must still match the source descriptions
They always make the project Group 10
They remove the architect’s classification role

questions.rationale: The classification rationale must connect facts to source group descriptions.
questions.explanation: Reverses the relationship; breadth of specialist consultants indicates higher, not lower, classification. Contradicts the framework which explicitly states that consultant coordination and integration of specialized expertise merit higher classification. Incorrectly limits consultant impact to Group 1; consultant breadth and depth influence classification across all groups—simple projects require few consultants, complex ones require many specialized experts. The breadth and depth of consultant coordination directly correlates with classification level. Projects requiring numerous specialized consultants merit higher classification than those requiring only basic structural and MEP consultants. The number and specialization of required consultants (theater systems, acoustics, IT, security, etc.) directly drive higher classification due to increased design coordination and integration complexity.

questions.text: What is the source-safe way to treat structural complexity?

options.text: As a possible complexity factor that must be tied to the source group descriptions
As a substitute for a fee computation

questions.rationale: Complexity matters, but the source descriptions still control classification.
questions.explanation: Ignores the explicit statement that structural sophistication 'profoundly influences classification' and treats building type as the sole determinant. Contradicts the framework which explicitly distinguishes between simple conventional structures and sophisticated systems like post-tensioned concrete, steel moment frames, and innovative systems. Incorrectly limits structural complexity impact to tall buildings, missing that a low-rise building with innovative or challenging foundations (waterfront, seismic zone, difficult soil) elevates classification equally. Structural sophistication profoundly influences classification. Simple cast-in-place concrete or light steel framing support lower groups, while sophisticated systems (post-tensioned concrete, steel moment frames, innovative systems) and site-specific structural challenges indicate higher classification. Structural system sophistication—from simple cast-in-place to post-tensioned, moment frames, or seismic-resistant design—is a major classification driver independent of building height.

questions.text: How should fast-track delivery be treated?

options.text: As a schedule/service condition to document, not a group change unless tied to a source classification rule

questions.rationale: Fast-track can affect management and service scope, but the checked source does not make it an automatic group trigger.
questions.explanation: Incorrectly assumes compressed schedule lowers classification; in fact, fast-track's intensive coordination and phased overlap increase classification. Treats delivery method as irrelevant when the framework explicitly states that delivery method influences classification; Design-Bid-Build differs fundamentally from Design-Build or CM at Risk. Overgeneralizes by assigning Group 10 automatically; fast-track elevates classification within the appropriate range for the project type, but does not guarantee Group 10. Fast-track projects demand intensive coordination, phased delivery, and value engineering involvement that elevate classification. Delivery method significantly influences classification decisions alongside building type and technical factors. Fast-track delivery method elevates classification because it requires overlapping design-construction phases, intensive coordination, and risk management beyond standard sequential Design-Bid-Build.

questions.text: How should a mixed-use building with an innovative facade and special consultants be classified?

options.text: By identifying use, complexity, constraints, and any special group description before choosing a group

questions.rationale: Source-safe classification requires facts tied to source group descriptions.
questions.explanation: Uses building height (4 stories) as the sole criterion, ignoring the innovation, LEED requirements, site constraints, and six specialized consultants that demand elevation. Vastly underclassifies a complex mixed-use project; Group 2 applies to simple residential, not projects with innovative facade, sustainability certification, and extensive consultant coordination. Automatically assigns the highest group regardless of actual complexity; Group 10 applies to exceptionally specialized projects, not all multi-factor scenarios. This project exhibits characteristics of multiple groups: mixed-use suggests Group 5 baseline; innovative design, sustainability requirements, challenging site access, and extensive specialist coordination elevate classification to Group 6 or 7. Synthesis of all factors is essential. Synthesize all factors (building type baseline, innovation, sustainability, site challenges, specialist count) to determine elevation; this 4-story mixed-use elevates from Group 5 baseline to Group 6–7.
